critical_findings.finding: Accidental public exposure of sensitive/private note content is likely if users deploy outputs to public static hosting, because access control is explicitly out-of-scope and there is no stated pre-publish safety rail (e.g., allowlist publish set, secrets scanning, or prominent warnings).

closure.closure_target: Before any public-deployment guidance is shipped (no later than M5), require an explicit safety mechanism and user-facing warning workflow.

critical_findings.finding: XSS/content injection in the generated static site can occur if Markdown raw HTML is passed through, if template rendering fails to escape user-controlled strings (titles/tags/link text), or if search UI renders snippets via innerHTML. This is high-impact in a trusted-user workflow because notes can include copied web content, and the output may be hosted/shared.

closure.closure_target: Before implementing full rendering + client-side runtime features (no later than M4), define and test the sanitization/escaping policy end-to-end.

closure.mitigation_expectation: Make safe-by-default behavior non-optional for MVP: disable raw HTML or sanitize it; escape all template insertions (including tags/link text); ensure search UI renders text nodes (not HTML); add regression tests with representative payloads.

closure.closure_target: Before committing to O1-only implementation optimizations (no later than M2 start), confirm scale and set enforceable performance/memory budgets plus stress tests.

closure.closure_target: Before implementing link graph/backlinks (M3), require explicit configured link syntax/precedence and add fixtures covering mixed-convention cases.

closure.closure_target: By M5 exit criteria, add deployment-target test matrix and enforce single URL-building helper across all generated links and runtime asset fetches.

critical_findings.finding: Output path overwrites or cross-platform breakage can occur due to slug/path collisions (e.g., multiple index.md), case-insensitive filesystems (macOS/Windows), Unicode normalization differences, or reserved filenames; this can silently drop notes or misdirect links/backlinks.

closure.closure_target: Before M3 (when canonical IDs are relied upon for graph correctness), implement collision detection and a deterministic disambiguation/error strategy; add Windows/macOS path fixtures.

closure.closure_target: By M1 exit criteria and before adding more derived artifacts (tags/search), add a repeat-build determinism check and remove timestamps/unstable ordering from outputs.

closure.closure_target: Before tag features (M2), define front matter parsing error policy (per-file warn/skip vs fail build), and add fixtures for malformed front matter.

critical_findings.finding: The build process, designed with an in-memory graph (Architecture Option O1), fails catastrophically (e.g., crashes from out-of-memory errors, hangs indefinitely, or becomes unacceptably slow) when processing a note collection at the upper end of the user's expected scale (related to Open Question Q3), rendering the tool unusable for its intended purpose.

A user inadvertently publishes a directory containing private or sensitive notes because the tool uses recursive discovery by default (R1) and robust exclusion mechanisms are not a guaranteed feature (R20 is a SHOULD). This leads to unintentional data leakage to the public internet, a severe risk given that access control is an explicit non-goal.

The Markdown rendering pipeline improperly sanitizes note content or allows raw HTML to pass through into the generated static site without adequate safeguards (Risk K7). This creates a stored Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerability, allowing malicious code to execute in the browser of anyone viewing the published site.

Due to ambiguous conventions for note identification (file paths vs. titles), linking, and tagging, the note graph is constructed incorrectly. This leads to silent data loss (overwritten pages due to slug collisions), broken links, and incomplete backlink/tag indexes, undermining the core navigation and discovery features.

The client-side search index, generated as a single monolithic artifact (R8), grows so large that it significantly delays page loads, consumes excessive browser memory, and causes the search UI to be unresponsive, failing the performance expectation defined in R22 for a moderately-sized note collection.

The build pipeline contains OS-specific logic, such as incorrect path separator handling, reliance on case-insensitive file lookups, or unacceptable character handling in filenames. This causes builds to fail or produce incorrect output when run on a different operating system than the one it was developed on (e.g., Windows vs. Linux/macOS).
